newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs approve new controls on biocides.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs approve new controls on biocides.

text.p: The European Parliament approved on Tuesday plans to introduce EU-wide rules controlling the sale in the single market of biocides like insecticides, fungicides and wood preservatives.

The aim of the draft directive -- COM(96)312 -- is to strike a balance between, on the one hand, protecting people and the environment from dangerous substances and, on the other, lifting the barriers to free trade in biocides by harmonising the different national rules for authorising their sale and use.

The parliament's environment committee voiced sharp criticism of the text as amended by the Council of Ministers, saying the chemical substances it covered were not properly defined and this could lead to different interpretations of what it actually covered.

Reporting for the committee, Danish Socialist Kirsten Jensen attacked the Council for not allowing parliament access to a series of related annexes specifying more clearly how the rules would be applied.
Parliament, which shared equal power with ministers to decide environmental legislation, could not judge the proposal properly if it did not have all the information, she insisted.
EU Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard said she also deplored the Council's habit of appending confidential statements to legislative texts.
But she urged Euro-MPs to approve the proposal to complete "the final link in a chain of legislation on chemical substances".

There are some 14,000 biocides on the market, some of which could have a devastating effect on the environment, water resources and human health, such as reducing sperm counts or creating hormonal problems.
The Danish commissioner said only biocides which had undergone "a thorough and full" risk analysis would be authorised in future.
These risk analyses would be based on information supplied by the biocides industry, Bjerregaard said.
In the event, the environment committee and the Green group failed to muster enough support radically to amend the proposal and it was given a second reading.
